name: Price Elasticity of Demand (Point)
description: Computes the point price elasticity of demand (dQ/Q)/(dP/P), the ratio of the proportional change in quantity to the proportional change in price. It measures how responsive quantity demanded is to a price change at a given point.
notes: The value is typically negative because demand falls as price rises; its magnitude above or below 1 signals elastic or inelastic demand. Uses point (base) values of Q and P, not midpoints.

name: Arc Price Elasticity (Midpoint Method)
description: Computes arc price elasticity by the midpoint method, dividing the change in quantity relative to the average of the two quantities by the change in price relative to the average of the two prices. It gives a single elasticity for a discrete move between two price-quantity points.
notes: Using averages as the base makes the result independent of the direction of change, unlike point elasticity. The value is usually negative for demand.

name: Income Elasticity of Demand
description: Computes the income elasticity of demand (dQ/Q)/(dI/I), the proportional change in quantity demanded divided by the proportional change in consumer income. It shows how demand for a good responds to income changes.
notes: A positive value indicates a normal good and a negative value an inferior good; a value above 1 marks a luxury. Q and I are the base levels used in the proportional changes.

name: Cross-Price Elasticity of Demand
description: Computes cross-price elasticity (dQx/Qx)/(dPy/Py), the proportional change in demand for good X divided by the proportional change in the price of good Y. It measures how the two goods relate in demand.
notes: A positive value indicates substitutes and a negative value complements; a value near zero means the goods are unrelated. Qx and Py are the base levels for the proportional changes.

name: Price Elasticity of Supply
description: Computes the price elasticity of supply (dQs/Qs)/(dP/P), the proportional change in quantity supplied divided by the proportional change in price. It measures how responsive producers' output is to price movements.
notes: The value is normally positive since supply rises with price; a magnitude above 1 is elastic supply. Qs and P are the base levels in the proportional changes.

name: GDP Deflator
description: Computes the GDP deflator nom/real*100, the ratio of nominal GDP to real GDP scaled to an index. It measures the overall price level of all domestically produced goods and services relative to the base year.
notes: Nominal and real GDP must be in the same currency units, with real GDP in base-year prices. A value of 100 marks the base year; above 100 indicates prices have risen since then.

name: Real GDP (from Deflator)
description: Computes real GDP nom/defl*100 by deflating nominal GDP with the GDP deflator index. It strips out price changes to express output in constant base-year prices, isolating the change in real production.
notes: The deflator is an index where the base year equals 100; nominal GDP is in current prices. Result is in the same currency units as nominal GDP but at base-year price levels.

name: Inflation Rate (CPI Change)
description: Computes the inflation rate (CPI2-CPI1)/CPI1*100, the percentage change in the consumer price index from a previous value CPI1 to a current value CPI2. It measures how much the general price level has risen over the interval.
notes: Result is already a percentage. A negative value indicates deflation; both CPI figures must be on the same index base for the comparison to be valid.

name: Quantity Theory of Money (Price Level)
description: Computes the price level M*V/Q from the quantity theory of money, where M is the money supply, V its velocity, and Q real output. Rearranged from MV=PQ, it shows the price level implied by the money stock and its circulation relative to output.
notes: Assumes the exchange equation MV=PQ holds with velocity and output given. M and Q must be in consistent units; V is the number of times money turns over per period.

name: Velocity of Money
description: Computes the velocity of money P*Q/M, how many times the money supply M turns over to finance nominal output (price level P times real output Q) in a period. It is derived from the exchange equation MV=PQ.
notes: P*Q is nominal GDP and M the money stock, in the same currency units. Velocity is a pure number per period; higher values mean each unit of money is spent more frequently.

name: Keynesian Spending Multiplier
description: Computes the Keynesian spending multiplier 1/(1-MPC), the factor by which an initial change in autonomous spending raises total equilibrium output, given the marginal propensity to consume MPC. A higher MPC produces a larger multiplier.
notes: MPC is a decimal between 0 and 1; here 1-MPC is the marginal propensity to save. The formula assumes a simple closed economy with no taxes or imports leaking from the spending cycle.

name: Tax Multiplier
description: Computes the simple tax multiplier -MPC/(1-MPC), the change in equilibrium output caused by a one-unit change in taxes, given the marginal propensity to consume MPC. It is negative because higher taxes reduce disposable income and spending.
notes: MPC is a decimal between 0 and 1. The tax multiplier is smaller in magnitude than the spending multiplier by one, since a tax change first affects income before it is spent.

name: Money Multiplier (Reserve Ratio)
description: Computes the simple money multiplier 1/rr, the maximum factor by which the banking system can expand the money supply from new reserves, given the required reserve ratio rr. A lower reserve ratio permits greater deposit expansion.
notes: rr is a decimal fraction of deposits held as reserves (0.1 = 10%). The formula assumes banks lend all excess reserves and no cash leaks from the system, so it is an upper bound.

name: Marginal Propensity to Consume
description: Computes the marginal propensity to consume dC/dY, the fraction of an additional unit of income that is spent on consumption. It captures how much of each extra dollar earned households choose to consume rather than save.
notes: Both changes should cover the same period; the result normally lies between 0 and 1. It is the slope of the consumption function and complements the marginal propensity to save (they sum to 1).

name: Marginal Propensity to Save
description: Computes the marginal propensity to save dS/dY, the fraction of an additional unit of income that is saved rather than spent. It measures how much of each extra dollar of income households add to savings.
notes: Both changes should cover the same period; the value normally lies between 0 and 1. It complements the marginal propensity to consume, with which it sums to 1.

name: Cobb-Douglas Production Function
description: Computes output from a Cobb-Douglas production function A*K^alpha*L^(1-alpha), combining capital K and labor L with total factor productivity A and capital share alpha. It gives total production under constant returns to scale.
notes: alpha is capital's output share, between 0 and 1, and the labor exponent 1-alpha is implied by constant returns to scale. K and L must be in consistent physical or value units.

name: Marginal Product of Labor (Cobb-Douglas)
description: Computes the marginal product of labor (1-alpha)*A*K^alpha*L^(-alpha) for a Cobb-Douglas technology, the extra output from one more unit of labor holding capital K fixed. It equals labor's share times average product per worker.
notes: alpha is the capital share; the labor exponent becomes -alpha here from differentiating with respect to L. Marginal product falls as L rises, reflecting diminishing returns to labor.

name: Marginal Product of Capital (Cobb-Douglas)
description: Computes the marginal product of capital alpha*A*K^(alpha-1)*L^(1-alpha) for a Cobb-Douglas technology, the extra output from one more unit of capital holding labor L fixed. In competitive markets it equals the real rental rate of capital.
notes: alpha is the capital share; the capital exponent alpha-1 comes from differentiating with respect to K. Marginal product declines as K grows, showing diminishing returns to capital.

name: Consumer Surplus (Linear Demand)
description: Computes consumer surplus 0.5*(Pmax-P)*Q for a linear demand curve, the triangular area between the choke price Pmax and the market price P over quantity Q. It represents the total benefit buyers gain above what they actually pay.
notes: Assumes a straight-line demand curve so the surplus region is a triangle; Pmax is the price at which quantity demanded reaches zero. All prices and quantity must be in consistent units.

name: Producer Surplus (Linear Supply)
description: Computes producer surplus 0.5*(P-Pmin)*Q for a linear supply curve, the triangular area between the market price P and the supply intercept price Pmin over quantity Q. It is the total gain to sellers above their minimum acceptable prices.
notes: Assumes a straight-line supply curve so the surplus is a triangle; Pmin is the price at which suppliers first enter (the vertical intercept). Prices and quantity must share units.

name: Deadweight Loss (Triangle)
description: Computes deadweight loss 0.5*dP*dQ, the triangular welfare loss from a market distortion such as a tax or price control, using the price wedge dP and the resulting reduction in quantity dQ. It measures gains from trade that go unrealized.
notes: Assumes linear supply and demand so the loss is a triangle; dP is the gap between the prices buyers and sellers face and dQ the fall in quantity traded. Both should be positive magnitudes.

name: Expectations-Augmented Phillips Curve
description: Computes inflation from the expectations-augmented Phillips curve pe - beta*(u-un), where expected inflation pe is adjusted by the response coefficient beta times the gap between unemployment u and its natural rate un. It links inflation to labor-market slack.
notes: Rates are decimal fractions. When unemployment exceeds its natural rate the gap term lowers inflation; when it falls below, inflation rises above expectations.

name: Okun's Law (Output Gap)
description: Computes the output gap from Okun's law -c*(u-un), relating the shortfall of output below potential to the gap between unemployment u and its natural rate un via the Okun coefficient c. It estimates lost output from cyclical unemployment.
notes: c is the responsiveness of output to unemployment (often around 2). A result below zero means output is below potential; u and un are decimal rates on the same basis.

name: Solow Steady-State Capital per Worker
description: Computes the steady-state capital per effective worker in the Solow growth model, (s*A/(n+g+delta))^(1/(1-alpha)), balancing savings s times productivity A against the effective depreciation from population growth n, technology growth g, and depreciation delta. It gives the long-run capital intensity the economy converges to.
notes: alpha is capital's share, so 1-alpha is labor's; all rates are decimals. The denominator n+g+delta is the break-even investment rate that just maintains capital per effective worker.

name: Marginal Revenue (Elasticity Form)
description: Computes marginal revenue P*(1+1/elast) using the price P and the price elasticity of demand elast. It expresses how revenue changes with one more unit sold, given that selling more requires a lower price along an elastic demand curve.
notes: elast is negative for a downward-sloping demand curve, so marginal revenue falls below price. Marginal revenue is positive only when demand is elastic (|elast|>1).

name: Lerner Index (Market Power)
description: Computes the Lerner index (P-MC)/P, the markup of price P over marginal cost MC as a fraction of price. It measures a firm's market power, with higher values indicating greater ability to price above cost.
notes: The result ranges from 0 under perfect competition (price equals marginal cost) toward 1 for strong monopoly power. P and MC must be in the same units.

name: Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (Two Firms)
description: Computes the Herfindahl-Hirschman index s1^2+s2^2 for a two-firm market, summing the squares of each firm's percentage market share. It gauges market concentration, rising as output concentrates in fewer firms.
notes: Shares are entered as percentages, so the index ranges up to 10000 for a pure monopoly. Squaring gives large firms disproportionate weight; a full market would include all firms' squared shares.

name: Consumer Price Index
description: Computes the consumer price index costt/cost0*100, the cost of a fixed basket of goods now relative to its cost in the base year, expressed as an index. It tracks the general price level faced by consumers over time.
notes: Both basket costs must be in the same currency for the same fixed basket; the base year equals 100. A value of 110 means prices are 10% above the base year.

name: Real Wage
description: Computes the real wage W/P*100, deflating the nominal wage W by a price index P to express earnings in constant purchasing-power terms. It shows what a wage can actually buy relative to the base year.
notes: P is a price index with the base year equal to 100, so the *100 restores base-year scale. The result is in base-year currency units, not a percentage.

name: Fisher Effect (Nominal Interest Rate)
description: Computes the approximate nominal interest rate r+inf from the Fisher effect, adding the real interest rate r and expected inflation inf. It shows the nominal rate that preserves a given real return once inflation is anticipated.
notes: Both r and inf are decimal fractions. This is the linear approximation; the exact Fisher relation adds a cross term r*inf, negligible only at low rates.

name: Quantity Theory (Inflation, Growth Form)
description: Computes the inflation rate gm+gv-gy from the growth form of the quantity theory of money, where money-supply growth gm plus velocity growth gv less output growth gy yields the price-level growth. It follows from differentiating MV=PQ.
notes: All inputs are growth rates as decimals. It assumes the exchange equation holds continuously; velocity growth gv is often taken as roughly zero over the long run.

name: Opportunity Cost Ratio (Production)
description: Computes the opportunity cost ratio good_a/good_b, the units of good A given up per unit of good B gained when reallocating production. It quantifies the trade-off along a production possibilities frontier.
notes: The result is how many units of A are forgone for each unit of B obtained; the reciprocal gives the opposite trade-off. Both quantities must reflect the same reallocation.

name: Terms of Trade Index
description: Computes the terms of trade index Px/Pm*100, the ratio of a country's export price index Px to its import price index Pm, scaled to an index. It shows how many imports a unit of exports can buy relative to a base period.
notes: Both are price indices on the same base (base = 100). A value above 100 means terms of trade have improved since the base period, so exports command more imports.

name: Marginal Rate of Substitution (Cobb-Douglas Utility)
description: Computes the marginal rate of substitution (alpha/beta)*(y/x) for Cobb-Douglas utility over goods X and Y, the rate at which a consumer will trade good Y for good X while holding utility constant. It equals the slope of the indifference curve at the bundle.
notes: alpha and beta are the utility exponents on goods X and Y; x and y are the current quantities held. The MRS diminishes as x rises relative to y, reflecting convex preferences.

name: Real Exchange Rate
description: Computes the real exchange rate by adjusting the nominal exchange rate for relative price levels, multiplying it by the ratio of foreign to domestic price levels. It expresses how many units of the domestic basket of goods trade for one foreign basket, reflecting real purchasing power.
notes: Convention depends on how the nominal rate is quoted (domestic per foreign vs. foreign per domestic); price levels should share a common base period. A rising value signals real depreciation of the domestic currency.

name: Unemployment Rate
description: Calculates the unemployment rate as the number of unemployed divided by the total labor force (unemployed plus employed), expressed as a percentage. It measures the share of people actively seeking work who do not have a job.
notes: The denominator is the labor force, not the whole population; people not seeking work are excluded entirely. Enter head counts (or consistent units) for both inputs.

name: Labor Force Participation Rate
description: Computes the labor force participation rate as the labor force divided by the working-age population, expressed as a percentage. It shows what fraction of the working-age population is either employed or actively looking for work.
notes: The labor force counts both employed and unemployed job seekers, so this differs from the employment rate. Both inputs must cover the same population definition (e.g., ages 15 and over).

name: Gini Coefficient (Two-Segment Lorenz)
description: Approximates the Gini coefficient of inequality from a Lorenz curve modeled as two straight segments through two kink points. The result is one minus twice the area under the piecewise-linear Lorenz curve, ranging from 0 (perfect equality) toward 1 (maximal inequality).
notes: This is a two-segment trapezoidal approximation, not the exact Gini; more kink points give better accuracy. Population and income shares must be cumulative, ordered, and lie between 0 and 1 with x1 < x2.

name: Compound Annual Growth Rate (Multi-Period)
description: Computes the compound annual growth rate (CAGR): the constant yearly rate that grows the initial value to the final value over n years. It is the n-th root of the final-to-initial ratio minus one, giving a smoothed annualized growth figure.
notes: The result is a decimal fraction (multiply by 100 for percent) and ignores intermediate volatility. Both values must be positive and n must be the number of years spanned, not the count of data points.
